title: Medical Committee for Human Rights v. SEC; SEC v. Medical Committee for Human Rights
citation: 432 F.2d 659 (D.C. Cir. 1970), vacated as moot, 404 U.S. 403 (1972)
lead: A shareholder campaign against Dow’s napalm production won a remand from the D.C. Circuit, but a later shareholder vote caused the Supreme Court to vacate that judgment as moot.

actors.name: Medical Committee for Human Rights
actors.role: Gift recipient of Dow shares seeking shareholder consideration of napalm production.

actors.name: Dow Chemical
actors.role: Corporation that sought to omit the proposal from proxy materials.

actors.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
actors.role: Federal agency whose full Commission approved staff’s no-action recommendation.

proceedings: The D.C. Circuit remanded the Commission determination for reconsideration in 1970. After Dow included the proposal and shareholders rejected it in 1971, the Supreme Court vacated the circuit judgment and ordered dismissal in 1972.
limits: The circuit opinion was vacated as moot, not approved or rejected on its merits. Its historical reviewability reasoning and former proxy-rule language are not statements of current law.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A gift of shares opens a dispute over napalm
paragraphs: The Medical Committee for Human Rights received stock in Dow Chemical by gift and sought to bring Dow’s napalm production before other shareholders. In March 1968 its chairman proposed a charter amendment prohibiting sales without assurances that the napalm would not be used against people. Alongside its humanitarian objection, the Committee asserted harm to employee recruitment and worldwide business. Dow said the proposal arrived too late for its 1968 proxy materials and promised later consideration.

Having heard nothing further, the Committee renewed its request in January 1969. Dow announced that it would omit the proposal. The Committee revised the request to ask directors to consider a charter amendment forbidding napalm manufacture, subject to federal defense-production requirements. The revised proposal sought directors’ consideration, rather than attempting to enact the amendment itself.

sections.title: The full Commission accepts a no-action recommendation
paragraphs: Dow invoked the Securities and Exchange Commission’s then-existing Rule 14a-8 exclusions for proposals primarily promoting general political or social causes and for ordinary business matters. The agency’s Division of Corporation Finance relied on Dow’s letter and counsel’s opinion in advising that it would recommend no action if Dow omitted the proposal.

The Committee retained counsel, requested review by the full Commission, and submitted legal arguments. The Commission approved the staff recommendation. Its minutes dated the decision March 24, 1969, but written notification was mailed April 2. The Committee petitioned for judicial review on May 29. The Commission contested jurisdiction rather than defending the substantive grounds for exclusion.

sections.title: The D.C. Circuit allows review of this Commission action
paragraphs: Judge Tamm wrote for a unanimous panel with Judges McGowan and Robinson. The Securities Exchange Act’s § 25(a) imposed a sixty-day review period, but the court rejected the agency’s reliance on the adoption date and telephone notification. The agency’s own rule contemplated availability for inspection, and written information had been unavailable for a substantial interval. An unexplained call could not fairly start the clock while depriving the shareholder of information needed to prepare review. The court did not need to decide whether the agency had waived timeliness by initially disclaiming the objection.

The Commission’s approved no-action position was reviewable because of its practical finality, impact, and procedural formality. The administrative process was complete. The Committee, a beneficiary of statutory corporate-suffrage protections, had expended effort pursuing it, lost possible agency assistance, and faced an adverse agency interpretation in any private suit. The existence of that separate remedy did not eliminate injury.

This was more than ordinary staff advice. Rule 14a-8 required an adversarial exchange in which management supplied the proposal, exclusion reasons, and legal support to both shareholder and agency; management bore the burden of establishing exclusion. The Commission had accepted the Committee’s submissions and made a final determination. The statutory scheme did not escape review because its principal enforcement method was an injunction rather than an administrative command. Direct appellate review also matched the requested relief: correction of a legal approach and reconsideration, without a fact trial or injunction requiring a district court. Forcing a private lawsuit would impose a circuitous, costly route on small investors.

sections.title: Review reaches legal premises without directing prosecution
paragraphs: The court distinguished discretion over enforcement resources from legal error. It did not treat negative agency action as categorically immune, or treat administrative discretion as all or nothing. Its concrete concern was that unexplained acceptance of management’s several objections gave the shareholder neither an intelligible decision nor guidance for future proposals.

The Commission had already elected to review this controversy. The court could therefore examine the legal framework and return the matter for an exercise of the discretion that remained. It would not supervise resource allocation, compel initial Commission review of every staff response, or order a particular enforcement action on remand. Review of the staff position depended on the Commission’s choice to take it up; this was no declaration that every staff no-action letter could be reviewed.

sections.title: Dow’s exclusion arguments require a better explanation
paragraphs: Section 14(a)’s corporate-democracy purpose guided the circuit court’s reading of the exclusions. The political-cause exception addressed proposals seeking consensus on matters unrelated to the company’s affairs. The ordinary-business exception preserved management’s routine operating authority, with state corporation law an important guide. Reading the exceptions to make every proposal either too general or too specific could defeat the inclusion rule.

Dow had not adequately identified controlling Delaware law or carried its burden. Delaware expressly permitted charter amendments changing the business’s nature, and Dow had not explained why this proposal fell outside that power. Opposition to the Vietnam War did not itself prove an impermissible political purpose: napalm was Dow’s own product. Even a socially motivated desire to accept lower profits supported a substantial argument for shareholder deliberation over corporate assets.

The record also suggested that management continued production for moral and political reasons despite limited profits and business costs. The court did not evaluate those choices’ wisdom; it questioned insulating management’s personal preferences from shareholder consideration. It remanded for reconsideration within the Commission’s proper discretion and a sufficiently detailed explanation, without ordering Dow to include the proposal. Rehearing was denied August 26, 1970.

sections.title: An intervening vote makes the Supreme Court case moot
paragraphs: Dow included a renewed proposal in its 1971 proxy materials. Less than three percent of voting shareholders supported it. Another agency rule then permitted exclusion of the same or substantially similar proposal for three years, although Dow maintained that it had been legally entitled to exclude it earlier.

Justice Marshall, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices Brennan, Stewart, White, and Blackmun, held the controversy moot. A new submission and rejection after that three-year interval were conjectural, especially given the scant support. Voluntary cessation would not moot likely recurring conduct, but the majority found no reasonable expectation of recurrence here. Article III therefore barred a merits ruling. On January 10, 1972 the Supreme Court vacated the appellate judgment and remanded to the court of appeals for dismissal. It neither affirmed nor rejected the circuit’s reviewability theory on the merits and did not decide the proxy exclusions’ substantive reach.

Justice Douglas dissented. Dow had retained the right to exclude future proposals and had not even promised to stop. Earlier voluntary-cessation decisions had found assurances insufficient; mere temporary cessation should not suffice here. A prediction that future inclusion would cost less than litigation was speculative and irrelevant to whether a live dispute remained. Douglas emphasized shareholder participation and possible agency rule changes strengthening management. Justices Powell and Rehnquist did not participate. The historical circuit analysis consequently carries the Supreme Court’s mootness vacatur with it.
